lessons.unit: Unit 1: Punctuation and grammar for stronger writing
lessons.title: Possessive apostrophes
objectives: Use apostrophes to show singular possession
Use apostrophes for plural possession, including irregular plurals

keywords.def: a mark (') that shows possession or missing letters
when something belongs to someone
one
more than one

starter: Bismillah. Write the plural: box, child, baby.
Punctuate: Come here said Mum.
Write a fronted adverbial of time.

teach.heading: What is possession?
teach.note: Show a picture of a coat and ask whose it is. Write 'the coat of the boy' then 'the boy's coat'. Explain that the apostrophe shows ownership.

teach.heading: One owner
teach.note: Practise with items in the room. Model with a name that ends in s: James's book (or James' book, either accepted in school). Warn about the common mistake of putting an apostrophe in plurals: apple's.

teach.heading: Many owners, plural with s
bullets: Add the apostrophe after the s
teach.note: Use a visual to show the difference: boy's (one boy) and boys' (more than one boy). Ask pupils which they would use for 'the books belonging to the girls'. They must decide first whether there is one or many owners.

teach.heading: Irregular plurals
bullets: the women's meeting, the men's coats
teach.note: Remind pupils that children, men, women and mice do not end in s, so 's is added. Show 'the childrens toys' is wrong and 'the children's toys' is right.

teach.heading: Test: who owns it?
bullets: Many owners ending in s: after s
teach.note: Give a quick-fire round. Show 'the dog's bones' (one dog) and 'the dogs' bones' (many). Check pupils understand the order of letters.

practice: Add the apostrophe: the cats bowl (one cat)
Add the apostrophe: the girls bags (more than one girl)
Correct: the childrens playground
independent: Rewrite ten phrases using an apostrophe (e.g. the hat of the king).
Write six sentences using possessive apostrophes.
Find the mistakes in a short paragraph and correct them.
exit: Which is correct: the boys' ball or the boy's ball (two boys)?
Write the possessive for the toys belonging to the children.
lessons.homework: Look for five examples of apostrophes for possession at home and write what they show.
lessons.send: SEND: use a one/many owner sorting sheet. EAL: practise with objects and pictures. Stretch: explain the difference between the dogs' and the dog's bowls.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Sinbad and the roc - reading and writing an adventure
lessons.title: Reading the adventure: Sinbad and the roc
objectives: Read a story and retrieve key facts
Summarise the main events in order

keywords.def: an exciting story with danger and risk
find information in a text
a short account of the main points
the order of events

starter: Bismillah. Replace with a pronoun: Sinbad was clever. Sinbad escaped.
Write a fronted adverbial of time.
Punctuate: Look shouted Sinbad.

teach.heading: Sinbad the Sailor
bullets: Each voyage brings danger and a clever escape
teach.note: Introduce Sinbad as a character from the collection of stories known as One Thousand and One Nights. Explain that today's version is a retelling. Ask pupils what they know about adventures at sea.

teach.heading: Read the story
bullets: Sinbad is left on an island
The roc carries him to a valley of diamonds
Merchants and eagles help him escape
teach.note: Sinbad woke to find that his ship had sailed without him. He was alone on a deserted island. Wandering inland, he came upon an enormous white dome, as smooth as marble. It was the egg of a giant bird called the roc! Suddenly, the sky grew dark as the roc returned to her nest. Sinbad was quick-witted. He unwound his turban and tied himself to one of her huge legs. At dawn, the bird soared into the sky and carried him across the sea. She landed in a deep valley where the ground sparkled with diamonds. But the valley was full of huge, hissing snakes! Sinbad hid in a cave until he saw merchants on the cliffs above hurling lumps of meat into the valley. Diamonds stuck to the meat, and eagles swooped down to carry it away. Sinbad filled his pockets with diamonds, strapped a piece of meat to his back and was lifted out of danger. Read aloud with drama, stopping after the egg to predict what happens.

teach.heading: Retrieving facts
teach.note: Model finding the answer to 'What was the egg like?' (as smooth as marble). Show how to underline the key words and use them in an answer.

teach.heading: Sequence the story
bullets: First: the ship sails without Sinbad
Next: he finds the egg and the roc
Then: the valley and the snakes
teach.note: Use time adverbials to order events. Ask pupils to retell the story in four sentences using a different time word each time.

teach.heading: Summarising
teach.note: Model a two-sentence summary. Check that the summary avoids detail such as the colour of the dome. Pupils write their summary on mini-whiteboards.

practice: Who or what is the roc?
How did Sinbad travel to the valley?
What lay on the ground of the valley?
independent: Answer six retrieval questions in full sentences.
Put eight events in order.
Write a four-sentence summary of the story.
exit: How did Sinbad escape from the valley?
Write one time adverbial you used in your summary.
lessons.homework: Retell the story in your own words to an adult, using at least three time words.
lessons.send: SEND: sequence cards with pictures. EAL: pre-teach deserted, enormous, soared. Stretch: write the story from the roc's viewpoint in three sentences.

lessons.title: Vocabulary in context and words ending -ous
objectives: Work out word meanings using context and root words
Spell words ending in -ous

keywords.def: the words around a word that help show its meaning
the main part of a word
a suffix meaning full of, as in dangerous
a book or tool that lists words with similar meanings

starter: Bismillah. Write the plural possessive: the merchants (ship).
Write a summary of the story in one sentence.
What is a pronoun?

teach.heading: Find the meaning
bullets: Read the sentence before and after
teach.note: Model with 'deserted': 'alone on a deserted island'. What clue helps? 'Alone' tells us nobody is there. Show how to try a replacement word and reread.

teach.heading: Key words from the text
bullets: quick-witted = clever and fast to think
teach.note: Pupils match words to meanings and use them in spoken sentences. Ask what other word could replace 'huge' in the story.

teach.heading: Words ending in -ous
teach.note: -ous means 'full of'. Explain the spelling rules: most words just add -ous; with a final e, sometimes the e drops (fame - famous) and sometimes it stays (courage - courageous). Learn the common ones.

teach.heading: Synonyms and a thesaurus
bullets: Choose the one that fits best
teach.note: Explain shades of meaning: 'huge' is bigger than 'large'. Use a thesaurus. Warn: check meaning in context, not just any word from a list.

teach.heading: Use new words
teach.note: Take pupil sentences. Praise accurate, imaginative usage. Link to appreciating Allah's creation when describing wonders in nature.

practice: What does 'hurling' mean in the sentence?
Spell: dangerous, famous.
Give a synonym for 'huge'.
independent: Match eight words to their meanings.
Write six sentences using words from the story.
Add -ous to five root words and spell them correctly.
exit: Spell the word meaning 'full of adventure'.
lessons.homework: Learn to spell: dangerous, famous, enormous, adventurous, mountainous.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards with images. EAL: use bilingual dictionaries for key words. Stretch: group words by shade of meaning and explain your order.

lessons.title: Character, inference and explaining our views
objectives: Infer what Sinbad is like from his actions
Support answers with evidence

keywords.def: work out something using clues
words from the text that prove an idea
a quality that a character shows, such as bravery
copy exact words from a text

starter: Bismillah. Spell: enormous, adventurous, famous.
What does 'soared' mean?
Write one synonym for 'clever'.

teach.heading: Inference
bullets: We work out meaning from clues
teach.note: Show a picture of a child with a frown and ask what they might feel. Link to inference: we use clues when authors do not tell us directly.

teach.heading: What is Sinbad like?
bullets: Quick-witted: he ties himself to the roc
Resourceful: he uses meat to escape
teach.note: Reread parts of the story. Ask which words show each quality. Model a full answer with quote: 'Sinbad is quick-witted because he unwound his turban and tied himself to the roc's leg.'

teach.heading: Using quotes
teach.note: Model embedding: Sinbad is clever because he 'unwound his turban'. Explain that we copy exactly. Pupils practise adding short quotes to their answers.

teach.heading: Fact and feeling
bullets: How might Sinbad feel in the valley?
teach.note: Ask pupils to consider his feelings from the situation, not only from words used. 'Hissing snakes' makes the scene threatening. Ask them to justify.

teach.heading: Writing your answer
teach.note: Model a three-part answer. Provide a sentence frame: 'I think..., because the text says '...'. This shows that...'.

practice: Find a word or phrase that shows Sinbad was clever.
How do you think Sinbad felt when he saw the snakes? Why?
What does the phrase 'hid in a cave' show?
independent: Write three P.E.E. paragraphs about Sinbad's qualities.
Find two quotes that show danger.
Write a comparison: Sinbad at the start and end of the extract.
exit: Write a quote that shows the valley was dangerous.
lessons.homework: Write a short character profile of Sinbad with evidence.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight evidence in the text and give frames. EAL: use word banks for qualities. Stretch: consider whether the merchants or Sinbad are more resourceful.

lessons.title: Writing a setting description
objectives: Use the senses to describe a setting
Use fronted adverbials, similes and noun phrases in description

keywords.def: where and when a story takes place
compares one thing to another using like or as
sight, sound, smell, touch, taste
the feeling a setting creates

starter: Bismillah. Write a sentence with a fronted adverbial of place.
Write an expanded noun phrase about a cave.
What is a simile?

teach.heading: What is a setting?
bullets: Where and when the story happens
Good description helps readers picture the scene
teach.note: Show a picture of a valley sparkling with diamonds and snakes among the rocks. Ask pupils how they would feel there. Link the setting to the mood: wonder and danger.

teach.heading: Use the senses
teach.note: Collect words for each sense. Model a sentence combining two senses: 'In the shadows, hissing snakes slithered over the cold, rough rocks.'

teach.heading: Similes
bullets: The valley sparkled like a sky full of stars.
teach.note: Explain that a good simile helps the reader imagine. Avoid clichés. Ask for fresh comparisons. Check there is a real similarity: 'sparkling like a sea of stars'.

teach.heading: Build a paragraph
teach.note: Model the paragraph: 'At the bottom of the valley, a carpet of glittering diamonds sparkled like frost in the sun. Beyond the rocks, hissing snakes coiled and uncoiled.' Underline the features.

teach.heading: Check it works
bullets: Have I used commas after fronted adverbials?
teach.note: Display a checklist and ask pupils to review their partner's sentences. Praise vivid, accurate phrases.

practice: Write one sentence describing the sound in the valley.
Complete the simile: The snakes were as long as...
Add a fronted adverbial: ____, the diamonds glittered.
independent: Write a paragraph describing the valley of diamonds using at least three senses.
Include a simile and two fronted adverbials.
Underline your best phrase.
exit: Write a simile for the roc's wings.
Which sense have you used most?
lessons.homework: Write a description of a place you know using three senses.
lessons.send: SEND: sense word bank and picture. EAL: label the picture first. Stretch: use a metaphor as well as a simile.

lessons.title: Planning our own voyage
objectives: Plan a new adventure episode in paragraphs
Choose a problem and clever solution

keywords.def: the events of a story
a group of sentences about one idea or event
the danger or challenge
how the character solves the problem

starter: Bismillah. Name two senses you use in description.
Write a simile about a mountain.
Punctuate: Help cried Sinbad.

teach.heading: An adventure plot
teach.note: Share a simple structure. Link each part to the story we read. Note that the problem should be solved by cleverness and courage, not just luck.

teach.heading: Our setting and danger
bullets: Choose a place: island, cave, desert
Choose a danger: storm, giant, beast
teach.note: Brainstorm in pairs. Collect ideas on the board. Warn pupils to keep the ideas realistic within the fantasy: the solution must use something Sinbad has or can find.

teach.heading: Plan in paragraphs
teach.note: Show a four-box plan. Explain that each paragraph deals with one stage and starts with a fronted adverbial. Model a plan: a desert storm, a hidden well, a camel caravan.

teach.heading: Plan the language
bullets: A fronted adverbial for each paragraph
teach.note: Model planning vocabulary: 'swirling sand', 'howling wind'. Ask pupils to choose three powerful words for each paragraph.

teach.heading: Share and improve
bullets: Tell your plan to a partner
Does the problem need a clever solution?
teach.note: Pairs share. Partner gives one star and one suggestion. Link to adab of listening: let your partner finish before responding.

practice: Choose your setting and danger.
Write a fronted adverbial for the start of your story.
Write the problem in one sentence.
independent: Complete a four-paragraph plan.
Write a list of ten powerful words for your story.
Write two lines of speech for your plan.
exit: State your problem and solution in two sentences.
lessons.homework: Improve your plan by adding detail to the solution.
lessons.send: SEND: use a plan with sentence starters. EAL: draw the four stages before writing. Stretch: add a surprise or twist in paragraph 3.
